about: RULES.md rule 3: the p1 and p2 verdicts of each row disagree (one keep, one not) and no counted third verdict decides the pair. A third judge sees the evidence and both judgements (judge_1 = p1, judge_2 = p2) and decides keep or revert.
pair_rule: A tie counts only while the p1 and the p2 verdict on the row's route are, as JSON records, the very pair it was shown: a round-1 tie the row's VERDICTS_RAW.json p1 and p2, a later round's tie the p1 and p2 on the route before that round (the pair TIE_ROUND<n>.json of the round before listed); once a later round replaces either, the tie is set aside as stale, and a pair that still disagrees needs a new tie.

judge_1.reason: This record is the gorge itself: its Wikidata P31 is 'defile' and it is described as a 'Limestone gorge'. The caves inside it have their own records (e.g. Aveline's Hole, typed Cave Structures), and so does the hillfort (Burrington Camp). A gorge is a natural feature, not a cave structure, so 'Natural feature' is the correct canonical type for this entity.

quotes.quote: Burrington Combe is a gorge through the limestone hills although there is now no river running through it.
Limestone gorge in north Somerset, England

judge_2.reason: Burrington Combe is a limestone gorge, but it is on an archaeological map because of its caves. These include Aveline's Hole, the earliest scientifically dated cemetery in Britain, and other cave entrances occupied for over 10,000 years; the stored description and card are about this too. 'Cave Structures' is the catalogue's canonical type for cave sites and is at least as well supported as 'Natural feature'. 'Natural feature' fits the landform but hides why the site is on the map. The change was not warranted.

quotes.quote: Various cave entrances are exposed which have been occupied by humans for over 10,000 years, with a hillfort being built beside the combe in the Iron Age.
The combe contains the entrances to many of the caves of the Mendip Hills, including Aveline's Hole, Sidcot Swallet and Goatchurch Cavern.
The earliest scientifically dated cemetery in Great Britain was found at Aveline's Hole.

The finder's reason fails, the old value is at least as well supported as Fortress/citadel, and the change was not warranted.

judge_1.reason: South Stoa I is a stoa built of poros foundations and mud-brick walls, so the stored 'Megalithic structures' is wrong. It was a utilitarian public building with offices and dining rooms for Athenian officials. The canonical list has no 'public building' type, and the catalogue already uses 'Infrastructure' for utilitarian public structures such as the Great Bath, a nymphaeum, a lighthouse and a cistern. A stoa counts as civic infrastructure in urban archaeology, so the written value is defensible.

quotes.quote: It probably served as the headquarters and dining rooms for various boards of Athenian officials.
construction suggests a utilitarian building.
stoa in the Agora of Athens

judge_2.reason: South Stoa I was a stoa in the Athenian Agora that housed magistrates' offices and dining rooms. 'Megalithic structures' (old) is wrong. 'Infrastructure' (written) is also wrong: in this catalogue that type sits in the Infrastructure group with roads, bridges, mines, quarries, canals and wells, and a civic colonnade building is none of those. The building was demolished around 150 BC and only its foundations survive, excavated by the ASCSA. 'Ruin' is the canonical type the same audit used for the comparable Stoa of Eumenes.

quotes.quote: It probably served as the headquarters and dining rooms for various boards of Athenian officials.

judge_1.reason: The site as named and described is the Late Bronze Age fortified settlement, occupied from the late 13th to the mid 12th century BC. -1300 is a round value in the correct '1500 - 500 BC' bucket; the old -3000 was in '3000 - 1500 BC', a different bucket. German Wikipedia also mentions Early Chalcolithic remains under the Aegean settlement, but the old -3000 does not match that phase either (Early Chalcolithic Cyprus is c. 3900-3500 BC), and no source gives that phase a year. So the old value is not better supported, and -1300 is right for the site this record describes.

So the site's securely attested start is about -3800, in the '4500 - 3000 BC' bucket. The old -3000 falls in the '3000 - 1500 BC' bucket, so it is wrong too.

The evidence shows otherwise: the site is a sanctuary about 80 x 80 m with successive temples (c. 570 BC, c. 500 BC, possibly a 7th-century one), an altar, a propylon, a cistern and a treasury. 'Temple' is defensible for the named building, but the old 'Temple complex' is at least as well supported.

judge_1.reason: The entity is a 310 km signposted tourist route. Wikidata P31 is Q23011975, 'paved road outside of settlements'. It links megalithic sites but is not itself a megalithic monument. One caveat for Martin: this is a modern route opened in 2009, and whether it belongs on the map at all is his content-scope decision, not a question of this field.

'Road/avenue/trackway' with that period would claim a Neolithic road that never existed. The old 'Megalithic stones' describes the archaeology the entry stands for and is at least as well supported.
